sides.text: Each router tells its directly connected neighbours all the networks it knows, along with its own distance to each

more.text: Sometimes called "routing by rumour" — a router has no topology information beyond what its neighbours have advertised.

sides.text: Each router describes itself and its directly connected interfaces/neighbours; this information is flooded unchanged to every router in the area

more.text: Every router ends up with the full topology and independently calculates the best routes from it.
Distance vector IGP. Uses hop count as its metric, max 15 hops. RIPv2 supports VLSM; RIPv1 does not. Rarely used outside very small or lab networks.
Cisco-proprietary, distance vector IGP (now obsolete). Calculates a composite metric from bandwidth and optionally delay, load, reliability and MTU. Superseded by EIGRP; doesn't support VLSM.
Originally Cisco-proprietary but now published. Advanced distance vector IGP, calculating a composite metric similarly to IGRP.
Link state IGP. Refers to OSPFv2 unless stated otherwise. Uses cost as its metric, automatically derived from interface bandwidth by default.
Link state IGP, used mainly in Service Provider networks. Its metric acts like hop count unless manually configured — it doesn't automatically factor in bandwidth.

sides.text: 1) Manually via router-id a.b.c.d 2) Highest IP of a loopback interface 3) Highest IP of a regular interface

more.text: Whichever rule matches first applies.

sides.text: Routers send Hello packets to multicast 224.0.0.5, containing their own RID and a list of RIDs already seen

more.text: After the initial Hello both routers are in Init state; once they've both seen each other's RID, they become 2-way neighbours.

sides.text: Full (fully adjacent) neighbours have exchanged Database Description packets (DBD) then any LSAs one has that the other doesn't, via Link-State Updates (LSUs)

more.text: Not all 2-way neighbours become full neighbours — see DR/BDR.

sides.text: Routers exchange Hellos continually at set intervals; if no Hello arrives within the Dead interval (a multiple of Hello) the neighbour is considered dead

more.text: The router(s) that noticed the failure flood LSAs reflecting the change so others update their LSDBs and recalculate routes.

sides.text: Routers reflood each LSA every 30 minutes by default, regardless of link changes

more.text: The refresh timer is separate per LSA, avoiding a network-wide surge from reflooding everything simultaneously.

sides.text: On a broadcast segment (e.g. Ethernet) with multiple routers, one is elected Designated Router and another Backup Designated Router; the rest become DROther

more.text: All routers become full neighbours with the DR and BDR (which act as hubs of information) but not with each other, reducing LSA traffic. DR/BDR are elected per broadcast network, not per router, and aren't used on point-to-point links.

sides.text: Highest OSPF interface priority wins DR, second-highest becomes BDR; highest RID breaks ties

more.text: Once elected there's no pre-emption — a new router joining, or a priority change, won't trigger a fresh election while the current DR/BDR are still up.

sides.text: Down → Init → 2-Way → Exstart → Exchange → Loading → Full
OSPFv2 supports IPv4 only; OSPFv3 supports both IPv4 and IPv6

more.text: OSPFv2 is commonly used in IPv4-only networks; OSPFv3 is required for IPv6.

sides.text: A single flat area means every router holds the full topology, which can exhaust router memory and forces a full reconvergence on any change

more.text: OSPF instead segments large networks into areas — a rule of thumb is up to 50 routers per area.

sides.text: Area 0 (backbone/transit area) carries all inter-area traffic by default; regular (nonbackbone) areas connect end users to the backbone

more.text: Small networks don't need this and can run everything in Area 0.

sides.text: An OSPF router with all of its interfaces in Area 0
A router with interfaces in multiple areas

more.text: Separates LSA flooding zones, is the primary point for (manually configured) area address summarisation, commonly sources default routes into its areas, and maintains a separate LSDB per connected area. Ideally connects to just two areas — the backbone plus one other — with three as the practical upper limit.

sides.text: A router with all of its OSPF interfaces in one, non-backbone area

more.text: Learns inter-area routes to other areas from its ABR.

sides.text: The inverse of a subnet mask — subtract each octet from 255

more.text: A 255.255.0.0 subnet mask becomes wildcard 0.0.255.255; a 255.255.255.252 mask becomes wildcard 0.0.0.3.

more.text: Useful when there's no other router on the segment, or when there's a foreign-organisation OSPF router present that shouldn't see your internal topology. passive-interface default makes all interfaces passive by default; no passive-interface ifname re-activates specific ones.

sides.text: Injects the router's own static default route into OSPF, making it an ASBR

more.text: The "always" keyword advertises the default route regardless of whether it's actually working.

Default reference bandwidth is 100 Mbps, so both FastEthernet (100 Mbps) and GigabitEthernet (1000 Mbps) round up to a cost of 1 — meaning OSPF treats all links ≥100 Mbps as equal unless the reference bandwidth is manually raised.

Provide redundancy for a subnet's default gateway, since a host can only configure one default gateway at a time

more.text: Two or more routers share a virtual IP (and virtual MAC); one is active and serves traffic, the rest are standby, with automatic failover if the active router fails.

The active router owns the virtual IP/MAC that hosts use as their default gateway; if it fails, a standby router takes over the virtual IP and MAC with no change needed on hosts. Configured per-interface with "standby group-id ip virtual-ip".

sides.text: Different subnets can use different routers as active, e.g. subnet A uses R1 active/R2 standby while subnet B uses R2 active/R1 standby

more.text: Spreads load across routers, unlike a single subnet where one router always handles all traffic.

Unlike HSRP/VRRP, load-balances traffic from a single subnet across up to four Active Virtual Forwarders (AVFs), coordinated by one Active Virtual Gateway (AVG) which answers ARP requests for the shared virtual IP with different AVFs' virtual MACs.
An open standard (unlike HSRP and GLBP), operating very similarly to HSRP, with one master router and one or more backup routers.

more.text: XX represents the group ID in hex; YY in GLBP is the AVF number.

sides.text: Routers forward traffic based on the Layer 3 destination IP address; switches forward based on the Layer 2 MAC address (Layer 3 switches are an exception)

more.text: IP addresses on a router are configured per physical interface (or subinterface), not per VLAN. Routers also have no MAC address table.

more.text: Faster interfaces are typically used for this purpose in modern networks instead.

more.text: If the check fails the route isn't added at all, even once the issue is fixed later — add the permanent keyword to override this.
Acts as a catch-all "last resort" route, typically sending traffic destined for the Internet out of the internal network.

sides.text: When multiple routes match a destination, the one with the longest (most specific) prefix is used

more.text: E.g. a /24 route to a destination wins over a matching /16 route, even though both technically match.

sides.text: When multiple routes exist to the exact same network and prefix, the one with the lowest Administrative Distance (0-255) is installed

more.text: The others are kept in their routing protocol's own database in case the preferred route is later removed.

more.text: RIP uses hop count; EIGRP uses "metric"; OSPF uses "cost" — both EIGRP and OSPF automatically factor in link bandwidth, unlike RIP.

sides.text: Each VLAN/IP subnet gets its own dedicated physical router interface

more.text: Rarely used in practice — you run out of router interfaces as VLANs grow, and routed traffic must physically travel to and from the router over Ethernet cabling.

sides.text: Multiple VLANs are trunked to a single router interface, with each VLAN routed via its own subinterface

more.text: Subinterfaces are named e.g. Gi0/0.10 and each needs encapsulation dot1q n (add the native keyword for the native VLAN) plus its own IP address.

sides.text: A switch that supports both Layer 2 frame forwarding and Layer 3 IP routing, using either SVI-based routing or routed physical ports (no switchport)

more.text: Requires sdm prefer lanbase-routing (on some models) plus ip routing enabled globally. This is the most common approach in modern networks since routing happens across the switch backbone instead of over external cabling.

sides.text: Requires both a route to the pinged host and a route back from that host to you

more.text: Entering "ping" with no parameters prompts for all parameters including source IP — useful for reverse route testing. Can use hostnames if a DNS server is configured.

sides.text: Shows every hop to a destination by manipulating a test packet's TTL, starting at 1 and incrementing until the destination is reached

more.text: IOS traceroute encapsulates UDP inside IP packets, while most other operating systems use ICMP echo requests — so the two can be differently affected by security rules on the path.
Initiates an outbound SSH session from EXEC mode.

sides.text: Can factor in delay, bandwidth, load and reliability, though by default only delay and bandwidth are considered

Neighbour table: directly connected routers, discovered via Hellos to multicast 224.0.0.10
Topology table: every route learned via EIGRP (not just the best ones), calculated with the Diffusing Update Algorithm (DUAL) to guarantee loop-free paths
Routing table: only the best route(s) per destination, called successors

Advertised/reported distance: the distance to the destination as reported by the next-hop router
Computed distance: reported distance plus this router's own distance to that next-hop router, used as the overall metric

more.text: The lowest (best) computed distance to a network is its feasible distance.

sides.text: A backup route with the second-best metric, kept in the topology table as a fallback for the successor

more.text: To qualify, its reported distance must be lower than the successor's feasible distance (the feasibility condition), guaranteeing a loop-free backup path. If the successor fails and there's no feasible successor, the router must query neighbours for a new one.

sides.text: Hello interval defaults to 5 seconds, Hold timer to 15 seconds

more.text: EIGRP messages use a specialised Reliable Transport Protocol at Layer 4, and EIGRP is protocol-independent — it can carry routes for Layer 3 protocols other than IP.

sides.text: maximum-paths sets how many equal-metric routes (up to 32, default 4) to install for Equal Cost load balancing

more.text: Unlike OSPF, EIGRP also supports Unequal Cost load balancing: the variance parameter (default 1) allows any path whose computed distance is less than feasible distance × variance and which satisfies the feasibility condition.

sides.text: Uses hop count as its only metric, with a maximum of 15 hops

more.text: Performs Equal Cost Multi-Path load balancing across up to 4 paths by default.

sides.text: RIPv1 doesn't send subnet mask info, so it can't support VLSM (all subnets in a network must share one mask) and sends broadcast updates every 30 seconds, with no authentication

more.text: RIPv2 supports VLSM, uses multicast 224.0.0.9 for updates, and supports authentication.
